## Example 5.1: Building enthalpies from a reference state

Air is heated in a steady-state duct heater from 25 $^\circ$C to 150 $^\circ$C at a
mass flow rate of 0.50 kg s$^{-1}$. $C_P = 1.01$ kJ kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$

Using a reference state of **air, gas, 0 $^\circ$C, 1 atm**:


1. Tabulate the absolute enthalpy of the inlet and outlet streams.
2. Calculate the required heat, $\dot{Q}$.

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Solution"}

**System and assumptions**

The system is the duct heater. Steady state, one stream in and one out, no work
($\dot{W}=0$), no phase change, no reaction. The general balance

$$\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = \sum \dot{m}_{in}H_{in} - \sum \dot{m}_{out}H_{out} + \dot{Q} + \dot{W}$$

collapses to

$$0 = \dot{m}H_{in} - \dot{m}H_{out} + \dot{Q}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\dot{Q} = \dot{m}\left(H_{out} - H_{in}\right)$$

**Part 1 — enthalpy relative to the reference state**

With $H_{ref} \equiv 0$ at $T_{ref} = 0\ ^\circ$C, each stream enthalpy is the sensible
heat needed to bring air from the reference temperature to its actual temperature:

$$H = \int_{T_{ref}}^{T} C_P\,dT = C_P\left(T - T_{ref}\right)$$

| Stream | $T$ ($^\circ$C) | $H = C_P(T - T_{ref})$ (kJ kg$^{-1}$) |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Inlet  | 25  | $1.01(25 - 0) = 25.25$ |
| Outlet | 150 | $1.01(150 - 0) = 151.5$ |

These are *not* absolute enthalpies of air in any physical sense — they are enthalpies
measured from the zero we chose.

**Part 2 — heat requirement**

$$\dot{Q} = \dot{m}\left(H_{out} - H_{in}\right) = 0.50\left(151.5 - 25.25\right)$$

$$\dot{Q} = 63.125\ \text{kW}$$

**Check**

The sign is positive, meaning heat is transferred *into* the system — correct for a
heater. The magnitude is plausible: a domestic fan heater is a few kW, an industrial
duct heater tens of kW.

Note also that $151.5 - 25.25 = 126.25$ kJ kg$^{-1}$, which is exactly
$C_P(T_{out} - T_{in}) = 1.01 \times 125$. The reference state cancelled — as it must.

**Using different reference states**

We could have also used a reference state of 25 or 200 $^\circ$C

*$T_{ref} = 25\ ^\circ$C*

| Stream | $T$ ($^\circ$C) | $H$ (kJ kg$^{-1}$) |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Inlet  | 25  | $1.01(25 - 25) = 0$ |
| Outlet | 150 | $1.01(150 - 25) = 126.25$ |

$$\dot{Q} = 0.50\left(126.25 - 0\right) = 63.125\ \text{kW}$$

Choosing the reference at the inlet temperature makes the inlet enthalpy **zero**, and it
drops straight out of the balance. This is the practical reason to choose a reference at
one of the stream temperatures.

*$T_{ref} = 200\ ^\circ$C*

| Stream | $T$ ($^\circ$C) | $H$ (kJ kg$^{-1}$) |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Inlet  | 25  | $1.01(25 - 200) = -176.75$ |
| Outlet | 150 | $1.01(150 - 200) = -50.5$ |

$$\dot{Q} = 0.50\left(-50.5 - (-176.75)\right) = 0.50 \times 126.25 = 63.125\ \text{kW}$$

**Comparison**

| $T_{ref}$ ($^\circ$C) | $H_{in}$ | $H_{out}$ | $H_{out} - H_{in}$ | $\dot{Q}$ (kW) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0   | 25.25   | 151.5 | 126.25 | 63.125 |
| 25  | 0      | 126.25 | 126.25 | 63.125 |
| 200 | -176.75 | -50.5 | 126.25 | 63.125 |

**What this shows**

- The individual enthalpies are completely different — and with $T_{ref} = 200\ ^\circ$C
  they are *negative*. A negative absolute enthalpy is not a physical impossibility; it
  simply means the state sits below the arbitrary zero we chose. It is the reference line
  in the figure moving up past both states, not the curve changing.
- The **difference** $H_{out} - H_{in}$ is identical in all three cases, so $\dot{Q}$ is
  identical. The reference state cancels algebraically:
  $C_P(T_{out} - T_{ref}) - C_P(T_{in} - T_{ref}) = C_P(T_{out} - T_{in})$.
- The choice is therefore free — but it must be applied **consistently**. Using
  $T_{ref} = 0\ ^\circ$C for the inlet and $25\ ^\circ$C for the outlet would give
  $0.50(126.25 - 25.25) = 50.5$ kW: a wrong answer.
